title: Unveiling the Power of Omega-3s in Reducing Inflammation: A Comprehensive Guide
abstract:
### Supplemental Options  
For individuals who may not consume enough omega-3s through their diet, **supplements** are an option. Common types include:  
- **Fish oil pills**: contain EPA (eicosapentaenoic acid) and DHA (docosahexaenoic acid) from processed fish fat.
- **Algal oil**: a plant-based supplement derived from algae, suitable for vegetarians and those who prefer not to consume fish products.  
Supplements come in various forms, such as soft gels, capsules, and liquids.
### Heart Health Benefits  
Omega-3 PUFAs, particularly eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), are linked to several cardiovascular benefits. They have been observed to **lower blood pressure** and **reduce triglyceride levels**, which can lead to a **reduced risk** of heart disease. The American Heart Association endorses the consumption of omega-3s for those at risk of coronary heart disease, as they can help prevent arrhythmias and decrease the likelihood of blood clots.  
- **Blood Pressure:**Regular intake of omega-3s is associated with healthy blood pressure levels.
- **Triglycerides:**These fatty acids can significantly lower triglycerides, important for heart health.
### Recommended Intakes  
The American Heart Association (AHA) recommends eating two servings of fatty fish per week for healthy individuals, which equates to approximately 500 mg per day of eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA). For those with high triglycerides, healthcare providers may suggest higher doses—between 2 to 4 grams per day of EPA and DHA from dietary supplements, under medical supervision.  
- **Adults with no history of heart disease:**Aim for at least two servings of fatty fish per week
- **Adults with coronary heart disease:**1 gram of EPA+DHA per day, preferably from oily fish
- **Adults with high triglycerides:**2-4 grams of EPA+DHA per day in the form of supplements
